Model quantifies value lost when anti-amyloid treatment is delayed

A U.S. microsimulation projected $104,885 in gross lifetime societal value per treated person and 32% more value when anti-amyloid treatment began two years earlier, but these are model-based gross benefits that exclude drug, screening and monitoring costs.

Key quantitative results: Treatment generated $104,885 in gross lifetime societal value per person (95% CI $99,291-$110,479), including quality-of-life gains, reduced unpaid caregiving and medical cost offsets driven largely by less nursing-home use and Medicaid spending.

ManagementDisease-modifying treatment access

Added October 8, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/alz.71819; PMID:42841389; PMCID:PMC13643942

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The model reframes diagnostic delay as potential loss of health, independence, caregiver time and public-program savings. Earlier treatment consistently improved projected value, but the headline figures are gross societal benefits—not cost-effectiveness ratios—and omit the costs required to find, confirm, infuse and monitor eligible patients. Results depend on assumptions about durability and whether earlier-stage efficacy is stronger.

Study design

Using a U.S. dynamic microsimulation, investigators modeled people resembling an early symptomatic Alzheimer trial population (mean baseline age 73.0 years). A treatment scenario slowed clinical progression by 29% over the remaining lifetime; an earlier scenario initiated therapy two years sooner. Outcomes included survival, disability-free time, community residence, quality of life, unpaid caregiving and medical spending, with sensitivity analyses for stronger early-stage efficacy and four-year effect duration.

Key quantitative results

  • Treatment generated $104,885 in gross lifetime societal value per person (95% CI $99,291-$110,479), including quality-of-life gains, reduced unpaid caregiving and medical cost offsets driven largely by less nursing-home use and Medicaid spending.
  • Starting treatment two years earlier increased modeled value by 32%. When the model also assumed 36% rather than 29% slowing in earlier disease, value was 71% higher than the trial-timing scenario.
  • With treatment benefit limited to four years, gross lifetime value fell to $49,122 for trial-timing treatment and $56,385 for earlier treatment. The model projected about 0.3 additional life-years, 1.0 fewer year with severe dementia, 0.37 disability-free years and 0.63 additional years in the community for the trial-timing treatment scenario.

What changed

A new U.S. model quantifies the potential societal cost of diagnostic and treatment delay and provides sensitivity ranges that health systems can compare with the real costs of screening, confirmation, infusion and monitoring.

Strength of evidence

Moderate modeling evidence for directional and scenario-based planning, grounded in trial efficacy and national data but not a prospective outcome or cost-effectiveness study. Conclusions are assumption-sensitive, particularly to duration of benefit, earlier-stage efficacy, treatment uptake and excluded implementation costs.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The findings support reducing avoidable diagnostic and treatment delays for otherwise eligible patients, while underscoring that implementation decisions require the omitted drug, biomarker, imaging, infusion, staffing and safety costs. The model should not be used to promise an individual benefit or to broaden treatment beyond labeled populations.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to access strategy, diagnostic-pathway investment, payer and health-system value discussions, and MSL questions about why earlier identification may matter even when clinical-trial efficacy is fixed.

Access or reimbursement relevance

High contextual relevance but no access action. The study quantifies potential value from shorter diagnostic and treatment delays; it does not establish coverage, reimbursement, capacity, assay availability or a funded care pathway.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Is $104,885 the net value after treatment costs?
No. It is gross societal value. Drug acquisition, diagnostic testing, infusions, MRI monitoring and implementation costs were not subtracted.
Does the model prove that every patient benefits more if treated two years earlier?
No. It projects population-average outcomes under specified assumptions and does not replace individual eligibility, risk-benefit assessment or observed clinical data.
Does this change coverage or eligibility?
No. It supplies an economic benchmark; FDA labeling, clinical guidance and payer coverage remain separate.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Microsimulation rather than prospective comparative outcomes
  • Gross value excludes drug, screening, biomarker, infusion and monitoring costs
  • Relies on assumed lifetime or four-year persistence of treatment effect
  • Earlier-stage efficacy scenarios are modeled rather than directly randomized
  • Results reflect U.S. costs, caregiving and Medicaid structures
  • Industry-related institutional funding and author relationships are disclosed

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record
